newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices propped up by lean heating oil stocks.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices propped up by lean heating oil stocks.

text.p: World oil prices eased slightly on Wednesday to just below a new five-year peak achieved earlier this week as new data confirmed the paucity of heating oil stocks on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean.

International benchmark Brent Blend crude, against which most westbound crude oils are priced, traded at $24.54 a barrel at 1703 GMT. This was four cents down on the day and 20 cents below the post Gulf War high of $24.70 reached on Tuesday.

The prompt crude contract made a renewed stab at attaining Tuesday's levels after a rumour swept the floor of the International Petroleum Exchange in London that President Boris Yeltsin of Russia, the world's third biggest oil producing country, was dead.
Brent for November delivery rose to a high of $24.62 a barrel before Yeltsin's office issued a statement that he was working at Barvikha Sanatorium, where he is awaiting a heart operation.

The main market mover in recent weeks with the approach of the northern hemisphere winter has been heating oil with stocks below levels deemed by analysts sufficient in the event of a protracted, cold winter.

Data issued this week on inventories of middle distillates (heating fuel and diesel) in the United States, the world's biggest energy consumer, showed stocks were 17.1 million barrels lower than the same week last year despite a slight build last week.

The picture was much the same in Europe, where higher prices have been drawing scarce heating oil from the U.S. market. Data released on Wednesday by Stitching Euroilstock also showed a deficit in European Union countries.
"The bottom line is that there is no respite for the market. The figures leave it terribly exposed to the weather," said Geoff Pyne, oil analyst at UBS bank.
"Distillates stocks (in Europe) are 20 million barrels short of comfort and crude 10 million barrels short. In the U.S. they are also 20 million barrels short of distillate," he added.

A trader for a major European oil company wondered how long the bull run would last, given the absence of any severe weather in Europe and temperatures seen improving after a cold snap in the high energy consuming area of the U.S. northeast.
"I think we've done enough for the time being and are likely to pull back again," the trader said, referring to five-year high gas oil futures on the IPE.

"We need some fundamental demand coming in like winter starting early. We have done a little bit too much to justify holding prices up. You can't follow through without some early sign of winter," he added.
